summary: Defines an LDAP schema, object classes and attributes for printers and print services, based on the Printer attributes of RFC 2911. It lets directories store printer information.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC tells a directory how to store information about printers. It defines a set of classes that a printer entry can belong to, and the attributes those classes hold, such as the printer's name, where it is, what paper it takes and how fast it prints. The attribute definitions are taken from the printing standards that already exist, so the directory entries line up with what printers report about themselves.

questions: what is the ldap printer schema
subtitle: A directory schema for describing printers, built on the attributes the printing standards already define.

tldr.problem: Directories can describe devices such as printers, but there was no schema telling a directory what a printer looks like, so every deployment invented its own attribute names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six LDAP object classes and around forty attribute types for printers, taking the attribute definitions from IPP/1.1, the Printer MIB v2, the IEEE 1284 Device ID command set and the IPP job and printer extensions.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational Independent Submission that obsoletes RFC 3712, the original LDAP Printer Schema. It registers new attribute types under an OID delegated to the IEEE-ISTO Printer Working Group.

today: RFC 7612 was published in June 2015 as an Informational Independent Submission and obsoletes RFC 3712, the original LDAP Printer Schema. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The document notes that all the object classes and most of the attribute types kept the object identifiers they had under RFC 3712, so existing directory data continues to work.

sections.title: What the Schema Is For
sections.content:
The document defines several object classes so that LDAP applications have flexible options in defining printer information using an LDAP schema. Classes are provided for directory entries with common printer information, and for extending existing directory entries with Service Location Protocol Version 2, Internet Printing Protocol version 1.1, and line printer protocol-specific information.

It is an Independent Submission to the RFC Editor by the Internet Printing Protocol Working Group of the IEEE-ISTO Printer Working Group, as part of the IPP Everywhere project for secure mobile printing with vendor-neutral client software.

The schema is technically aligned with the stable IANA-registered service:printer v2.0 template, for compatibility with already-deployed SLPv2 service advertising and discovery infrastructure. The attribute syntaxes are also aligned with that template, so simpler types are sometimes used, for example DirectoryString rather than labeledURI for the printer-uri attribute.

The RFC explains where the attribute definitions come from. The schema is based on all the printer attributes listed in Appendix E of the IPP/1.1 model and semantics document that are defined in its section on printer description attributes, plus selected attributes defined in Printer MIB v2, the PWG Command Set for IEEE 1284 Device ID, IPP Job and Printer Extensions Set 3, and IPP Everywhere.

The OIDs have a history. In March 2000 IBM permanently assigned ASN.1 OIDs to all the object classes and attribute types defined in the original LDAP Printer Schema, RFC 3712. In October 2011 IBM permanently delegated the base OID 1.3.18.0.2.24.46 to the IEEE-ISTO Printer Working Group for use in any PWG project, and in the same month the PWG permanently assigned subordinate OIDs for the new attribute types this document defines.
sections.plainLanguage: The printing world already had detailed descriptions of what a printer can do, in the printing standards themselves. This RFC takes those descriptions and turns them into something a directory can store, so that an application can look up a printer in the directory and learn the same things it would learn by asking the printer directly.

sections.title: The Object Classes
sections.content:
The RFC defines six LDAP object classes for use with both generic printer-related information and services specific to SLPv2, IPP/1.1 and LPR. They are slpServicePrinter, an auxiliary class for SLP-registered printers; printerAbstract, an abstract class for all printer classes; printerService, a structural class for printers; printerServiceAuxClass, an auxiliary class for printers; printerIPP, an auxiliary class for IPP printers; and printerLPR, an auxiliary class for LPR printers.

The abstract class defines the common printer attributes that are not specific to any one type of service, protocol or operating system. The structural class derives from it and inherits those attributes, and can be used with or without auxiliary classes to define printer information. The auxiliary class also derives from the abstract class and inherits the same attributes, but is used to extend other structural classes that already describe a printer, so it adds printer-uri and printer-xri-supported without the need for a second structural class. When extending other structural classes, the RFC notes that printerService should not be used. The slpServicePrinter class defines information specific to SLPv2 and is derived from slpService, the parent class for all SLP services. The IPP class extends structural classes with IPP-specific information, and the LPR class identifies directory entries that support LPR and requires the printer-name attribute.

The RFC gives four examples of how applications could combine the classes: use printerService for entries with common printer information; use printerService together with slpServicePrinter for printers registered with SLP; use printerService, printerLPR and printerIPP for printers supporting both LPR and IPP; and use printerServiceAuxClass together with object classes not defined by this document to extend other structural classes that describe printer information. Attribute names are used instead of OIDs in the class definitions for clarity, and some attribute names from IPP/1.1 have been prefixed with printer- to address the flat namespace for LDAP identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: One class holds everything a printer has in common, and it cannot be used on its own. A second class is the usual one to put on a printer entry. Two more auxiliary classes add the address of the printer and the ways it can be reached. The last two add the details specific to IPP printing and to the older line printer protocol.

sections.title: The Attribute Types
sections.content:
The attribute types are the values a printer entry can hold. They come from four sources. The largest group comes from IPP/1.1, including printer-uri, printer-xri-supported, printer-name, printer-natural-language-configured, printer-location, printer-info, printer-more-info, printer-make-and-model, printer-ipp-versions-supported, printer-multiple-document-jobs-supported, printer-charset-configured, printer-charset-supported, printer-generated-natural-language-supported, printer-document-format-supported, printer-color-supported, printer-compression-supported, printer-pages-per-minute, printer-pages-per-minute-color, printer-finishings-supported, printer-number-up-supported, printer-sides-supported, printer-media-supported, printer-media-local-supported, printer-resolution-supported, printer-print-quality-supported, printer-job-priority-supported, printer-copies-supported and printer-job-k-octets-supported.

Selected attributes come from Printer MIB v2, such as printer-current-operator, printer-service-person, printer-delivery-orientation-supported, printer-stacking-order-supported and printer-output-features-supported, along with printer-aliases. The Command Set for IEEE 1284 Device ID supplies printer-device-id, and IPP Job and Printer Extensions Set 3 supplies printer-device-service-count, printer-uuid, printer-charge-info, printer-charge-info-uri, printer-geo-location and printer-ipp-features-supported.

The RFC sets out how the values are meant to be handled. For compatibility with existing implementations and with underlying string length limits in other specifications, implementations should not exceed those limits, to avoid truncation and false matches. For interoperability and consistent display, values should be normalized as recommended for network interchange, should not contain DEL or any C0 or C1 control characters except for horizontal tab, carriage return and line feed, should only contain carriage return and line feed together rather than as singletons, and should not contain those three characters in names such as printer-name and printer-aliases. Some attributes are described as a list of values with a comma as the member delimiter and others as a single value, but in all cases any attribute can have multiple values represented as multiple instances, except where the syntax restricts it to be single-valued.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the attributes are the ones the printing standards already define, renamed with a printer- prefix so they do not collide with other names in a directory. A few come from a network management standard, one from the command set a printer uses to identify itself, and a handful are new. The RFC also says how long values may be and which control characters should not appear in them.

sections.title: Syntaxes and Matching Rules
sections.content:
The document defines no new attribute syntaxes and no new matching rules. It reuses the ones from the directory string definitions, and lists the three syntax OIDs it refers to: Boolean, DirectoryString with UTF-8 encoding, and Integer. The five matching rules it refers to are booleanMatch and integerMatch for equality, caseIgnoreMatch for equality, integerOrderingMatch for ordering, and caseIgnoreSubstringsMatch for substring matching.

The RFC gives its reasons for choosing them. DirectoryString is used for three groups of attributes: URI attributes such as printer-uri, printer-xri-supported, printer-more-info, printer-charge-info-uri and printer-uuid, whose UTF-8 encoding is compatible with internationalized resource identifiers; description attributes such as printer-name, printer-location, printer-info and printer-make-and-model, whose UTF-8 encoding supports descriptions in any language; and keyword attributes such as printer-compression-supported, printer-finishings-supported, printer-media-supported, printer-media-local-supported and printer-print-quality-supported, which are compatible with the union syntax used in IPP/1.1.

Case-insensitive equality matching is used for the URI attributes in order to conform to the spirit of the URI standard, which requires case-insensitive matching on the host part of a URI but case-sensitive matching on the rest of it. Either choice is a compromise: case-sensitive whole-URI matching can lead to false negative matches and has been shown to be fragile, since deployed client applications tend to tidy up host names in a URI, while case-insensitive whole-URI matching can lead to false positive matches, and publishing URIs that differ only by case is dangerous. For description and keyword attributes, case-insensitive matching is simply more user-friendly, and for the IEEE 1284 Device ID attributes it is mandatory. Case-insensitive substring matching is chosen for the same reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema reuses the standard string and number types and the standard rules for comparing them, rather than inventing new ones. The one interesting choice is that names and addresses are compared without regard to case, which makes searching easier, with the exception of the printer's own device identifier, where the rules are stricter.

sections.title: Registration of the OIDs
sections.content:
The document defines no new syntaxes or matching rules. It defines a few new attribute types, which have been registered by IANA, and notes that all the object classes and most of the attribute types were already registered by IANA when RFC 3712 was published.

The seven new attribute types were assigned by the IEEE-ISTO Printer Working Group under the delegated base OID and registered with IANA: printer-device-id at 1.3.18.0.2.24.46.1.101, printer-device-service-count at 1.3.18.0.2.24.46.1.102, printer-uuid at 1.3.18.0.2.24.46.1.104, printer-charge-info at 1.3.18.0.2.24.46.1.105, printer-charge-info-uri at 1.3.18.0.2.24.46.1.106, printer-geo-location at 1.3.18.0.2.24.46.1.107 and printer-ipp-features-supported at 1.3.18.0.2.24.46.1.108.

The section on the classes and attribute types from RFC 3712 is strictly informative; none of those OIDs were re-registered. The object classes carry the OIDs assigned by IBM: slpServicePrinter at 1.3.18.0.2.6.254, printerAbstract at 1.3.18.0.2.6.258, printerService at 1.3.18.0.2.6.255, printerServiceAuxClass at 1.3.18.0.2.6.257, printerIPP at 1.3.18.0.2.6.256 and printerLPR at 1.3.18.0.2.6.253.
sections.plainLanguage: Each class and attribute has a number, an object identifier, that names it globally. The six classes and most of the attributes kept the numbers they had in the earlier schema, so existing directory data still works. Seven attributes are new and got numbers under a block that was handed to the printer working group for its own use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the LDAP authentication guidance for details on authentication methods and on the use of TLS to supply connection confidentiality and data integrity for LDAP sessions. It also notes that security vulnerabilities can arise if DEL or any C0 or C1 control characters are included in names, such as printer-name or printer-aliases, and points to the security considerations for deploying printers in an IPP environment.

The main point is about access control. As with any LDAP schema, it is important to protect specific entries and attributes with the appropriate access control. It is particularly important that only administrators can modify entries defined in this printer schema. Otherwise, an LDAP client might be fooled into diverting print service requests from the original printer or spooler to a malicious intruder's host system, thus exposing the information in printed documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The danger is not to the directory but to the print jobs. If anyone can change a printer entry, they can point it at their own machine and receive whatever is printed, so the entries have to be writable only by administrators and the connection should be encrypted.
